near_miss.why_not: Norse rau-do gulli concerns precious gifts; its Greek partners concern inflamed eyes and temple decoration, not gold with this epithet. Root-pair searches found Slavic red gold, recorded separately as a search lead; the apparent cognate red root in those hits belongs to rust, not the adjective.

Norse fara í nótt and Greek night movement are ordinary military scheduling; Serbian night travel concerns illumination by jewels. Night is cognate, but the travel predicates differ and the shared circumstances do not establish inherited wording.

Night watch and remaining awake have congruent military settings, but the supplied partners lack the same predicate plus night collocation. Searches for wake-root plus night returned OHG Christian usages; targeted Latin/Vedic/epic search returned no hits. No distinctive cross-branch formula established.

The Norse exhortation is poetically distinctive, but neither the Irish apple/blossom passage nor Latin tree-management passage shares the weapon image. Red/bloom-root searches mainly returned plants and literal redness; Sanskrit rudhira searches returned ordinary blood imagery, and red-root plus asi yielded no hit. No verified cross-branch inherited collocation.

Norse feðr né mǿðr coordinates recipients of showing a ring; Irish máthir and athir are members of a longer list of relatives surrendered. Sanskrit pitṛ-gṛham and mātuḥ are not a coordinated parent pair. Natural family enumeration is insufficiently distinctive.

Norse liggja and Old Russian лежащю are cognate, as are the night nouns, and both narratives concern armed parties. But ordinary overnight lodging requires exactly these words; there is no marked syntax or poetic figure. Wider search gives commonplace lying/night combinations and Christian three-days/three-nights language. No inheritance claim.
The Norse mother is the giver of advice to another person’s father; Greek coordinated genitives identify shared parents. These are not the same syntactic pairing.

Norse going to sleep at night and Herodotean night-time sleeping are natural narrative circumstances. Homer has the more distinctive sleepless-nights expression, absent from the Norse passage. Root identity alone does not establish inheritance.

Norse tunga is geographical land between waters, and þurfa is need; Latin lingua torpet describes the bodily tongue becoming numb. No common collocation. The Latin root mapping also conflates stiffness with satisfaction.

The Norse naming of a child has no corresponding naming collocation in its supplied Homeric or Herodotean partners. Search found Latin nomen dare, recorded separately. A transparent naming idiom with a renewed verb remains weak evidence by itself.

near_miss.lead: Father and mother with birth or descent
near_miss.why_not: Norse legal status derives from the parents’ outlawry; Homer speaks of Achilles’ exalted parents; Herodotus discusses parentage and parricide; Latin describes children dying on parents. Cognate kinship terms recur, but no distinctive inherited phrase with congruent syntax and context emerges.

Norse describes tears, whereas Greek supplied partners describe rain, river flooding, or sailing. Eye/water searches yielded washing, baptism, and other physical water contexts, with no verified cross-branch tear formula. No equation based solely on water and flow roots.

Both Norse and Vedic preserve cognate masculine/feminine animal terms. Vedic coordinates threats in a protective prayer; Norse ylgr receives ulfs beitu in battlefield praise, not a masculine/feminine coordinated merism. Sanskrit epic describes escape from wolves’ bodies. Morphological inheritance does not establish shared phraseology.

search_lead.cognate: Norse gull and Russian золото continue related gold formations in *ǵhelh3-. Norse rauðr and Russian красный are not cognate; the adjective is a possible renewal.
search_lead.argument: An epithet plus gold pairing: rau-do gulli in a gift and красно золото in a proverb about non-rusting gold. Worth comparison as traditional precious-metal diction, but the late Russian witness and ordinary colour description make inheritance uncertain. The search red-root hit is actually ржавфетъ, not Красно; this is not an exact two-root match.

search_lead.cognate: Norse nafn and Latin nomen continue *h1nomn; gefa and dare represent different verb roots.
search_lead.argument: Both use give plus name, with a recipient; Norse names a child, while Plautus announces the title of a comedy to the audience (the next line supplies it). A possible renewed naming construction, but transparent semantics and the different naming situations make this a weak lead, not an inheritance claim.
